strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: efficient RoI identification for fine-grained MLLM perception, avoiding both costly annotation-based training and slow/multi-pass training-free attention methods.

The proposed pseudo-label generation pipeline (sink-token removal via feature norm, confidence-based label assignment with ignored ambiguous regions) is a sensible and empirically validated way to denoise noisy attention maps, with clear ablations showing each component's contribution.

The RPN design is architecturally efficient—reusing/initializing from frozen middle layers of the backbone and requiring only a single partial forward pass—which is a genuinely useful systems-level contribution distinct from prior multi-pass or autoregressive-decoding-based methods.

Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks (Document/OCR and vision-centric/high-resolution) and multiple backbones (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL 1.3B/7B), showing consistent and often large improvements over both a training-based (S2) and training-free (ViCrop) baseline.
Good data efficiency demonstration: substantial gains even with only 10K training samples, and generalization to unseen benchmarks (TextVQA, DocVQA, V-Star) not directly used in training.
Extensive ablations (backbone depth, RPN depth, data size, smoothing strategy, upscaling strategy, self-generated vs. GT-based labels) that lend credibility to design choices.
Reasonably reproducible: hyperparameters, layer configurations, and algorithmic pseudocode are provided in the appendix; prompts are given; evaluation done via a standard library (lmms-eval).
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to older/smaller MLLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL); no experiments on more modern, stronger architectures (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL-3.0) which are prominently discussed in the introduction/related work, raising questions about generalization to models with different attention structures or higher native resolution handling.

The theoretical justification in Appendix E is a fairly generic noisy-label/regression-to-conditional-expectation argument (essentially restating that averaging reduces variance) and does not tightly connect to the specific design choices (e.g., why selective classification with an ignore region outperforms plain regression is asserted more than formally derived beyond the general MSE argument).

Throughput comparisons are only reported on a single GPU type (A6000) and are relatively coarse; it is unclear how sensitive efficiency gains are to different hardware, batch sizes, or when combined with modern optimized inference stacks (e.g., FlashAttention, KV-cache reuse) that might change the relative overhead of multi-pass baselines.

The novelty of individual components (self-distillation, attention-sink removal, region proposal networks) is somewhat incremental — each idea builds directly on established techniques (Kang et al. 2025a/b, Zhang et al. 2025, Shao et al. 2025); the contribution is more of a careful, effective combination/engineering pipeline than a fundamentally new mechanism.

No comparison with VILA-HD or other full pretraining-based RoI methods is given (only S2 and ViCrop), despite VILA-HD being repeatedly cited as a key related/competing approach in the introduction; this omission limits the completeness of the comparison landscape.

The paper reports results on a single run per configuration without variance/error bars, which is a concern given ablation deltas (e.g., V* changes of only a few points between adjacent data-size or layer settings) could be within noise given relatively small benchmark sizes (e.g., V*-Bench).

Some of the qualitative examples (Fig. 5) appear cherry-picked success cases without failure-case analysis, making it hard to assess when/why the RPN might mis-localize or hurt performance (e.g., for multi-object or distributed queries).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: avoiding costly annotation and slow multi-pass/auto-regressive RoI identification for fine-grained MLLM perception.
Extensive ablation studies (backbone depth B, RPN depth R, data scale, pre/post smoothing, label assignment vs. raw attention) that attempt to isolate the contribution of each pipeline component.
Consistent empirical improvements over the chosen baselines (LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL-1.3B/7B) across several Document/OCR and vision-centric benchmarks.
Demonstrated data efficiency, with meaningful gains using only 10K training samples.
Reasonably detailed implementation description (Algorithm 1, hyperparameter tables) aiding reproducibility of the described pipeline.
weaknesses: Key related training-based competitor VILA-HD, explicitly discussed in the introduction and related work as a primary motivating baseline, is never empirically compared against — only S2 and ViCrop are used as baselines, which weakens the central claim that SD-RPN 'resolves' the annotation-vs-efficiency trade-off relative to the strongest prior work.

All experiments are run on relatively old/weak backbones (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL); despite extensively motivating the work with modern MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL-3.0) in the introduction, the method is never validated on these stronger, more relevant architectures that already use dynamic/native resolution, making it unclear whether the reported >10% gains would hold or are simply exploiting the weak fixed-resolution baseline's known deficiencies.

The method still incurs a substantial throughput cost relative to the no-RoI baseline (0.62x–0.40x across models) and the efficiency advantage over ViCrop, while present, is incremental rather than transformative given the added training/pipeline complexity (pseudo-label generation, per-model layer search, multiple thresholds).

Per-model hyperparameters (selected attention layers, frozen backbone depth B) in Table 6 appear to be manually tuned per architecture via ablation search rather than derived from a principled or automatic criterion, raising concerns about generalization effort and reproducibility when applying the method to new models.

The theoretical justification in Appendix E is a generic noisy-label/regression-to-the-mean argument (conditional expectation reduces variance) that is not specific to this setting and does not provide rigorous support beyond standard intuition already motivated empirically in Fig. 3.

Core technical ingredients (sink-token removal via feature norm, ignoring ambiguous middle-confidence pseudo-labels, self-distillation from middle-layer attention) are largely drawn from or closely resemble prior work (Kang et al. 2025a/b, ViCrop), making the overall novelty feel like a combination/engineering of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new contribution.
Qualitative results (Fig. 5) are presented as cherry-picked success cases with no failure-case analysis or discussion of when/why the RPN mislocalizes, limiting insight into robustness.
No variance/error bars are reported for results, particularly concerning in the low-data (10K sample) regime where training stochasticity could be significant.

The throughput/accuracy trade-off and the method's generalizability to video or multi-object/multi-region scenarios (mentioned as future work) are not empirically explored, leaving the scope of applicability narrow.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: balancing the cost of training-based RoI methods against the inefficiency of training-free attention-based methods.

The pseudo-label generation pipeline (sink-token removal + selective label assignment with ignored ambiguous tokens) is a sensible and well-ablated denoising strategy, with Table 3 clearly showing the incremental contribution of each component.

Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks (Document/OCR and Vision-Centric/High-Resolution) and across two different MLLM families (LLaVA-1.5 at 7B/13B and DeepSeek-VL at 1.3B/7B), suggesting some generality of the approach.
Impressive data efficiency, achieving large gains with only 10K training samples and no external annotations, which is a meaningful practical advantage.
Thorough ablation studies (backbone depth, RPN depth, smoothing strategy, upscaling strategy, data scale, teacher response source) that support the design choices and improve reproducibility.
The self-distillation design (reusing self-generated responses rather than stronger external teacher responses) is an interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive finding that is empirically validated.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to relatively older/smaller MLLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL); no results on more modern, already high-resolution-capable models mentioned in the intro (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL-3.0), which limits confidence that the method's benefits persist on stronger baselines already handling fine-grained perception better.

Comparison methods are limited to S2 and ViCrop; no comparison to training-based RoI methods like VILA-HD or other recent perception-token-based approaches (Yu et al. 2025, Shao et al. 2025) that are discussed in related work, making it hard to judge SD-RPN's relative positioning against the full landscape of competing approaches.

The throughput gains are modest and the method is still substantially slower than the baseline (e.g., 0.62x, 0.51x, 0.40x-0.47x throughput), so the 'efficiency' claim is relative only to other two-stage RoI methods, not to standard single-pass inference; this nuance could be stated more prominently.

The theoretical justification in Appendix E relies on simplistic noise models (class-conditional noise, additive activation model) that are not validated empirically against the actual attention noise characteristics, so it functions more as a plausibility argument than rigorous proof of superiority.

Several hyperparameters (τ_norm, τ_fg, τ_bg, layer selections, backbone depth B) appear to be manually tuned per model (Table 6), raising concerns about how much additional tuning would be needed to extend the method to new architectures, partially undercutting the 'annotation-free, lightweight' practicality claims.

The reported '10% absolute accuracy improvement' headline claim is driven by a subset of benchmarks (e.g., DocVQA, V-Star) while gains on other benchmarks (ChartQA, InfoVQA) are much smaller, so the abstract's framing may overstate the general magnitude of improvement.

No analysis of failure cases or scenarios where the predicted RoI might miss relevant regions (e.g., multiple disjoint objects, very large foregrounds), despite acknowledging the Box vs Masked upscaling trade-off qualitatively.

strengths: Addresses a clear and practical bottleneck: efficient RoI identification for fine-grained MLLM perception without expensive annotation or slow multi-pass/auto-regressive decoding.

The pseudo-label generation pipeline (sink-token removal via feature norms + selective label assignment with ignored ambiguous regions) is well motivated by an empirical analysis (Fig. 3) showing that mid-range attention scores are unreliable, and ablations (Table 3) convincingly show each component contributes incremental gains.

Extensive experimentation across multiple MLLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL-1.3B/7B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B) and many benchmarks (Document/OCR and Vision-Centric/High-Res) demonstrates broad applicability and consistent, often large, absolute improvements.
Strong data efficiency claim is supported: only 10K-152K samples needed, and gains hold even at 10K, which is appealing relative to training-heavy competitors like VILA-HD.

Thorough ablation studies covering backbone depth, RPN depth, thresholds, upscaling strategy, smoothing strategy, and an interesting counter-intuitive finding that self-generated responses outperform ground-truth SFT responses as distillation targets.

Efficiency analysis is reasonably detailed, including throughput comparisons, comparison against Grounding-DINO as an external grounding baseline, and performance-throughput trade-off curves against naive resolution scaling.

Good transparency: appendix includes algorithm pseudocode, layer-selection rationale per model, failure case analysis, and a theoretical justification (though somewhat informal) for why denoised label learning beats raw attention regression.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical' justification in Appendix F is a fairly generic bias-variance/regression-to-mean argument (E[A|X] has lower MSE than raw A) that doesn't specifically justify why the proposed discrete label-assignment/ignore-region scheme is better than continuous regression on denoised attention (in fact Table 3's #2 'Attention Prediction' ablation already denoises via a learned regressor and label assignment further helps, suggesting the theory doesn't fully explain the specific design choice of discretization vs continuous regression).

The core novelty is somewhat incremental: combining known ideas (sink-token removal from ViT-register literature, self-distillation, an RPN-like read-out head on frozen middle-layer features) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the main contribution is a careful/practical pipeline rather than a conceptual breakthrough.

The throughput drop of SD-RPN (0.4x-0.6x of baseline) is still substantial, and while it's faster than ViCrop/S2 in relative comparisons, the paper doesn't fully justify why the two-stage approach is preferable to end-to-end training-based methods (VILA-HD) in raw accuracy despite the annotation-free claim, since no direct head-to-head accuracy comparison with VILA-HD is given.

Some benchmarking comparisons appear favorable to the paper but may not be entirely apples-to-apples (e.g., baseline LLaVA-1.5 numbers reported here, such as 21.5 on DocVQA and 18.1 on ChartQA, seem unusually low relative to commonly reported LLaVA-1.5 numbers in the literature, raising reproducibility/fairness concerns about baseline configuration).

The comparison with reinforcement-learning based methods (DeepEyes, Thyme) in Table 2 only includes results on Qwen2.5-VL-7B for a subset of benchmarks and directly copies numbers from original papers (marked with †) rather than re-running under the same evaluation harness, which could introduce inconsistencies given the paper explicitly notes it re-implemented other baselines for fairness.

The threshold selection (τfg=0.2, τbg=0.1 as default, later 0.05) appears heavily hand-tuned via grid search on validation performance without clear guidance on how these transfer to new datasets/domains beyond the ones tested, raising concerns about generalizability of hyperparameters.

The qualitative failure-case analysis (Fig. 9) reveals notable weaknesses in spatial relationship reasoning after cropping, suggesting the RoI-cropping paradigm itself may harm certain types of question that require global context, but this limitation is not thoroughly quantified or addressed with a mitigation strategy.
Code availability link is empty in the abstract, limiting current reproducibility verification despite claims of full reproducibility via lmms-eval.

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: balancing annotation cost, training cost, and inference efficiency for RoI-based high-resolution MLLM perception.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL 1.3B/7B, Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B) and many benchmarks (DocVQA, ChartQA, OCRBench, InfoVQA, TextVQA, V*, POPE, HR-Bench), showing consistent, often large, accuracy gains.

Thorough ablation studies covering pseudo-label denoising components (sink-token removal, label assignment), backbone/RPN layer depth, data scale (down to 10K samples), threshold tuning, and smoothing strategy, which help isolate the contribution of each design choice.

Reasonable efficiency analysis showing the RPN's single middle-layer forward pass is faster than training-free multi-pass attention baselines (ViCrop) and an external grounding model (Grounding-DINO), supporting the claimed efficiency advantage of feature reuse.
Data efficiency claim (10K samples yielding double-digit gains) is a meaningful practical contribution if it holds up, reducing the barrier to applying the method.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Appendix F is a fairly standard/elementary statistical argument (conditional expectation minimizes MSE under additive/CCN noise) that does not actually match the paper's real training procedure (masked binary classification with ignored ambiguous tokens), making it feel like post-hoc padding rather than a rigorous analysis of the proposed method.

Per-model hyperparameters (selected attention layers, frozen backbone depth B) vary substantially across architectures (e.g., B=9 for DeepSeek-VL-1.3B vs B=21 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B), suggesting the method requires non-trivial, architecture-specific tuning that undercuts claims of a simple, generalizable recipe.

Gains on the strongest baseline (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) are comparatively modest (~3% on text-rich benchmarks), raising questions about diminishing returns as base MLLMs improve, which is important given the field's trajectory toward stronger native dynamic-resolution models.

Baseline numbers (e.g., LLaVA-1.5-7B DocVQA of 21.5) appear considerably lower than commonly reported figures in prior literature, and all competing methods were re-implemented by the authors in-house; this raises reproducibility and fairness concerns about whether baselines were optimally configured.
No code link is actually provided (placeholder left empty), undermining reproducibility despite claims of a fully specified, simple pipeline (Algorithm 1).

Absolute performance after applying SD-RPN to LLaVA-1.5 still lags well behind other SoTA high-resolution methods (Monkey, Mini-Gemini-HD, LLaVA-TokenPacker-HD) in Table 11, which somewhat weakens the practical significance of the proposed enhancement despite the relative improvement framing.

The explanation for why self-generated responses outperform GT-response-derived pseudo-labels ("representational consistency") is intuitively argued but not rigorously validated beyond a single ablation row; alternative explanations (e.g., simpler/shorter self-generated answers producing more peaked attention) are not ruled out.

Throughput reductions (0.4–0.6x of baseline) are still substantial in absolute terms, and the efficiency comparison with S2 (a full-tuning method) is somewhat apples-to-oranges since S2 is not primarily an RoI-prediction technique.

Qualitative failure case analysis (Fig. 9) reveals persistent issues with incomplete activation, localization errors, and spatial relationship errors that are not deeply addressed or quantified in the main results, leaving open how often such failures occur at scale.

strengths: Tackles a well-motivated and practical problem: efficient, annotation-free RoI identification for fine-grained MLLM perception, resolving the training-cost vs. inference-latency trade-off of prior approaches.

The pseudo-label generation pipeline is carefully designed and empirically justified (e.g., Fig. 3's analysis of attention-score vs. localization-accuracy motivates the selective binary labeling and sink-token removal steps).

Architecturally efficient design: the RPN reuses the MLLM's own middle-layer features via a partial forward pass, avoiding costly multi-pass prefill or autoregressive decoding used by prior training-free RoI methods.

Extensive empirical validation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL 1.3B/7B, Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B) and many benchmarks (Document/OCR, vision-centric, high-resolution), with consistent and often large gains.
Thorough ablation studies covering pseudo-label components, backbone/RPN layer depth, data scale, smoothing strategy, and foreground/background thresholds, which support the design choices.

Additional comparisons against external grounding models (Grounding-DINO) and recent RL-based methods (DeepEyes, Thyme) as well as token-compression SoTA baselines, situating the method well within the broader literature.

Good transparency: includes qualitative successes, a dedicated failure-case analysis categorizing error types, and a theoretical appendix justifying why learned RoI prediction should outperform raw attention.
Demonstrated strong data efficiency (10K samples sufficient for large gains), which is a practically valuable property.
weaknesses: The per-model hyperparameters (selected attention layers, frozen backbone depth B) in Table 7 appear to require substantial architecture-specific tuning, which somewhat undercuts the claimed scalability/generalization of the approach and is not deeply analyzed for transfer across models.

Throughput gains are more modest than the headline efficiency claims might suggest in some configurations (e.g., 0.4-0.6x of baseline throughput), and the overall two-stage pipeline (RoI prediction + cropping + re-encoding + extended generation) still adds non-trivial system complexity relative to a single forward pass baseline.
Comparisons with RL-based methods (DeepEyes, Thyme) are limited to a single model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and likely differ in training data/scale, making the comparison not fully controlled.

Table 11's cross-method comparison mixes differences in base LLM, training data size, and max resolution, which complicates isolating the specific contribution of SD-RPN versus the underlying backbone's capacity.
The failure-case analysis is only qualitative (a handful of examples) without a quantitative breakdown of failure-mode frequency, limiting insight into the method's robustness.

Pseudo-label generation still requires running the full MLLM's autoregressive decoding plus attention extraction during training-data preparation, which, while a one-time cost, is non-negligible and not deeply quantified in terms of total pipeline cost.
No variance/multiple-run statistics are reported, so the robustness of the reported improvements to run-to-run variability is unclear.
